Kaka did recover though, and it's something that the deeply religious Brazilian has put down to the help of God, and ever since has given some of his income to his Church. Once recovered, he didn't waste time in getting his career restarted. By January 2001 he had made his debut in the Sao Paulo senior team and led the team to its first Torneio Rio-Sao Paulo championship. The following year he was a part of the Brazil team which won the 2002 FIFA World Cup, and in 2003 his talents had attracted the interest of European clubs and he signed to AC Milan for euro 9 million ($12 million) per season, and remains under contract with them through 2013. Since then he's won the Serie A, UEFA Champions League and FIFA Club World Cup with AC Milan, while on a personal level he won the 2007 Ballon d'Or Award for the best player in Europe and the FIFA World Player of the Year 2007 -- among many other awards. His international performances have continued to be strong -- and he has now scored 23 goals for Brazil. Such is his influence inside and outside of football, that Kaka was named in the Time 100 most influential people in 2008. Outside of the game Kaka has continued to be a devout Christian. He married his long-time partner Caroline Celico in 2005, and they had their first child in June 2008. Oddly, the current season (in which he finds himself being offered the biggest football salary ever) hasn't been as profitable for Kaka. The 26-year-old has struggled with a groin injury and has not managed to combine as smoothly within the AC Milan team compared to previous seasons. Still, that did not seem to worry Manchester City -- or Real Madrid, and for now at least, the $150 million transfer effort remains the biggest in football's history.

LONDON, England (CNN) — He is the player who has just turned down wage proposals reportedly worth as much as $700,000 per week. But who exactly is Kaka, and what has he achieved to command such extraordinary sums?

Kaka, whose full name is Ricardo Izecson dos Santos Leite, was born in Brazil in 1982 and is best known as a footballer for Italian side AC Milan. His nickname is thought to have originated with his brother, who could not pronounce “Ricardo” properly and instead called him “Kaka.”

Regarded as an exceptional prospect from early childhood, the attacking midfielder joined Sao Paulo when he was only eight years old. Before reaching his 16th birthday, he had already agreed to his first professional contract.

At one stage, however, what seemed like a promising career was put in serious doubt. In 2000, when Kaka was 18, he was injured in a swimming pool accident and fractured a vertebra in his spine. The damage was so severe that some feared it might not only end his football career but also leave him unable to walk.

Kaka eventually made a full recovery, something the deeply religious Brazilian has credited to God. Since then, he has donated part of his earnings to his church.

After returning to fitness, he quickly resumed his progress. In January 2001, he made his first appearance for Sao Paulo’s senior team and helped guide the club to its first Torneio Rio-Sao Paulo title. A year later, he was included in the Brazil squad that won the 2002 FIFA World Cup.

By 2003, his ability had drawn attention from clubs in Europe, and he moved to AC Milan for 9 million euros, or about $12 million, per season. His contract with the club runs until 2013.

During his time with Milan, Kaka has helped the team win Serie A, the UEFA Champions League and the FIFA Club World Cup. Individually, he has collected numerous honors, including the 2007 Ballon d’Or as Europe’s best player and the 2007 FIFA World Player of the Year award.

He has also remained an important figure for Brazil, scoring 23 goals for the national team. His standing both in football and beyond was underlined in 2008, when Time magazine included him in its list of the 100 most influential people in the world.

Away from the pitch, Kaka has continued to be known for his strong Christian faith. He married his longtime partner, Caroline Celico, in 2005, and the couple welcomed their first child in June 2008.

Curiously, the season in which he has been linked with the largest salary offer in football history has not been his most successful. Now 26, Kaka has been troubled by a groin injury and has not fitted into AC Milan’s play as seamlessly as he had in earlier campaigns.

Even so, that did not appear to deter Manchester City — or Real Madrid. For the moment, the attempted $150 million transfer remains the biggest offer in the history of football.

**Kaka: The Brazilian superstar who said no to Manchester City’s millions**

At the height of his powers, Ricardo Izecson dos Santos Leite — known worldwide simply as **Kaka** — was more than a footballer. He was a symbol of elegance, faith and attacking brilliance; a player whose smooth stride and devastating acceleration made him one of the most admired figures in the sport.

In January 2009, he also became the face of one of football’s most dramatic transfer sagas, when **Manchester City** tried to make him the centerpiece of a new era of unprecedented spending.

City, newly backed by Abu Dhabi wealth, wanted to sign the AC Milan playmaker in a deal that would have shattered records. Reports at the time suggested the English club was prepared to offer Milan a transfer fee of around **£100 million** and pay Kaka wages that could have reached roughly **£500,000 a week** — an extraordinary sum in the football market of the late 2000s.

Kaka turned it down.

“I wanted to stay at Milan,” he said at the time, choosing loyalty and stability over a move that would have made him one of the highest-paid athletes on the planet.

## Who is Kaka?

Born in Brasília in 1982 and raised in São Paulo, Kaka came through the ranks at **São Paulo FC**, where his talent quickly marked him out as one of Brazil’s brightest young players. Tall, quick and technically refined, he was not a traditional Brazilian dribbler in the mold of Ronaldinho or Neymar. His game was built on timing, vision, power and direct running.

He could glide past midfielders, split defenses with passes and arrive in the box like a striker. At his best, he made elite football look effortless.

Kaka moved to **AC Milan** in 2003, joining a team full of established stars, including Paolo Maldini, Andrea Pirlo, Clarence Seedorf and Andriy Shevchenko. He did not take long to become central to one of Europe’s great clubs.

## Why did Manchester City want him?

Manchester City’s pursuit of Kaka was about more than signing a brilliant player. It was about making a statement.

In 2008, City had been taken over by the Abu Dhabi United Group, transforming the club’s financial power overnight. The club wanted to accelerate its rise from Premier League hopefuls to global giants. Signing Kaka — then one of the most marketable and successful players in the world — would have announced City’s arrival at the very top level.

On the pitch, he was exactly the type of player any ambitious side would covet: a world-class attacking midfielder in his prime, capable of changing matches on his own. Off the pitch, he carried global appeal. He was a World Cup winner, a Champions League hero and a Ballon d’Or recipient with a clean-cut image that sponsors loved.

For City, Kaka would have been both a footballing upgrade and a declaration of intent: proof that the club could attract the biggest names in the sport.

## What had Kaka achieved?

The proposed salary was enormous, but Kaka’s record helped explain why City was willing to go so far.

With **Brazil**, he was part of the squad that won the **2002 FIFA World Cup**, becoming a world champion at just 20. He later became a key figure for the national team, representing Brazil at multiple major tournaments.

With **AC Milan**, his achievements were even more defining. Kaka helped the club win the **Serie A title** in 2004 and became the driving force behind Milan’s run to the **2007 UEFA Champions League** title. That season remains the peak of his career.

In the 2006-07 Champions League campaign, Kaka was sensational. He finished as the competition’s top scorer and delivered decisive performances against elite opposition, including Manchester United in the semifinals. Milan went on to defeat Liverpool in the final, avenging their famous loss in Istanbul two years earlier.

His performances earned him football’s most prestigious individual honors. In 2007, Kaka won the **Ballon d’Or** and the **FIFA World Player of the Year** award, beating contemporaries such as Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi. At a time when Ronaldo and Messi were about to dominate the sport for more than a decade, Kaka was the last player before their era to stand clearly above the rest.

## Why did he reject the offer?

Kaka’s refusal was striking because of the size of the offer and the direction football was moving. City had the money, Milan was under pressure and the deal appeared possible. But Kaka was deeply attached to Milan and wary of leaving for a club that, at the time, had not yet become the powerhouse it is today.

His decision was celebrated by Milan supporters, who had protested against the potential sale. For them, Kaka was not just an asset; he was the club’s golden boy, the player who represented Milan’s status at the summit of European football.

The move never happened. Later in 2009, Kaka did leave Milan — but for **Real Madrid**, one of the few clubs with a history and profile to match his stature.

## His legacy

Injuries later reduced some of Kaka’s explosiveness, especially during his time in Spain, but they did not erase what he had already achieved. At his peak, he was one of the finest attacking midfielders of the modern era: graceful, decisive and devastating in transition.

Manchester City wanted him because he represented everything the club hoped to become — elite, global, glamorous and feared. The salary offer reflected not only his ability, but his status.

Kaka rejected the money, and in doing so added another layer to his reputation: a superstar who, at least in that moment, chose belonging over a record-breaking payday.

**Kaká Chooses Legacy Over Riches as Manchester City’s Millions Fail to Lure Milan’s Golden Boy**

In an era when football’s financial landscape is shifting at dizzying speed, Ricardo Izecson dos Santos Leite — known to the world simply as Kaká — has offered a reminder that not every superstar can be bought.

The Brazilian playmaker has turned down a staggering offer from Manchester City, rejecting the chance to become the face of the Premier League club’s ambitious new project. Backed by enormous wealth and determined to build a global powerhouse, City identified Kaká as the ultimate statement signing. The proposed deal would have made him one of the most expensive and best-paid footballers in history.

But Kaká said no.

For AC Milan supporters, it was more than a transfer decision. It was a declaration of loyalty from a player who has become a symbol of elegance, humility and devotion — both on and off the pitch.

---

### From Brasília to São Paulo: The Making of Kaká

Born on April 22, 1982, in Brasília, Kaká grew up in a comfortable, close-knit family. His father, Bosco Izecson Pereira Leite, was an engineer, and his mother, Simone dos Santos, was a teacher. Unlike many Brazilian footballers who emerge from poverty, Kaká’s background was relatively privileged, but his rise was shaped by the same ingredients that define great athletes: discipline, faith and extraordinary talent.

His nickname came from his younger brother Rodrigo, who struggled to pronounce “Ricardo” and called him “Caca,” which later became Kaká.

As a child, Kaká moved with his family to São Paulo, where he joined São Paulo FC’s youth system. His technical ability, balance and vision soon marked him out as a special prospect. Yet his career almost ended before it had truly begun.

At 18, Kaká suffered a serious spinal injury after a swimming pool accident, fracturing a vertebra. Doctors warned that his future in football could be in doubt. Kaká recovered fully — a comeback he has long described as a blessing from God — and returned with renewed purpose.

That experience became central to his identity. For Kaká, football was never merely a profession. It was a calling.

---

### Rising Star at São Paulo

Kaká made his senior debut for São Paulo in 2001 and quickly became one of Brazil’s brightest young talents. Tall, quick and technically gifted, he was not a traditional Brazilian No. 10 in the mould of a Ronaldinho or Rivaldo. His game was more direct: gliding runs through midfield, precise passing, late arrivals in the box and a devastating ability to accelerate away from defenders.

His performances earned him a place in Brazil’s squad for the 2002 World Cup. Though he played only a minor role, Kaká was part of the team that lifted the trophy in Japan and South Korea, alongside Ronaldo, Rivaldo, Ronaldinho, Cafu and Roberto Carlos.

By then, Europe was watching.

---

### AC Milan and the Birth of a Superstar

In 2003, AC Milan signed Kaká from São Paulo for a fee that would soon look like a bargain. He arrived in Italy as a promising 21-year-old. He soon became one of the best players in the world.

Under Carlo Ancelotti, Kaká flourished in a Milan side packed with experience and intelligence: Paolo Maldini, Andrea Pirlo, Clarence Seedorf, Gennaro Gattuso, Andriy Shevchenko, Alessandro Nesta and Filippo Inzaghi. In that environment, Kaká’s gifts were given structure.

His first season brought the Serie A title. More importantly, it announced the arrival of a player who could decide games at the highest level.

Kaká’s style made him one of football’s most watchable stars. He carried the ball with long, graceful strides, seeming to cover ground faster than defenders could react. He was powerful without appearing forceful, creative without being showy, and clinical without being selfish.

At Milan, he became the bridge between midfield and attack — the heartbeat of Ancelotti’s system.

---

### Istanbul Pain and Athens Glory

Kaká’s Milan career has been shaped by two Champions League finals.

In 2005, Milan led Liverpool 3-0 at half-time in Istanbul, with Kaká producing a majestic first-half performance. His pass to Hernán Crespo for Milan’s third goal remains one of the great assists of the modern Champions League era. But Liverpool staged a stunning comeback and won on penalties, leaving Milan and Kaká devastated.

Two years later, redemption arrived.

In 2007, Kaká was the outstanding player in Europe. He drove Milan through the Champions League with decisive performances, including a memorable display against Manchester United in the semi-finals. His goals at Old Trafford and San Siro underlined his status as the tournament’s dominant force.

Milan defeated Liverpool 2-1 in the final in Athens, and Kaká finished as the Champions League’s top scorer. That year, he won the Ballon d’Or and the FIFA World Player of the Year award, beating Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi at a moment when the next era of football greatness was just beginning.

For many, 2007 was Kaká’s coronation.

---

### Faith at the Centre

Kaká’s public image has always been inseparable from his Christian faith. After major victories, he has often revealed shirts bearing messages such as “I belong to Jesus.” He has spoken frequently about prayer, gratitude and purpose, and he has credited his recovery from the spinal injury as a turning point in his spiritual life.

In a sport often associated with ego and excess, Kaká has cultivated a reputation for modesty. He rarely courts controversy. He speaks calmly, avoids inflammatory headlines and presents himself as a family man as much as a football icon.

His faith has not been a marketing tool but a consistent part of his life and career.

---

### Family and Private Life

Kaká married his childhood sweetheart, Caroline Celico, in 2005. Their relationship has been closely followed in Brazil and Italy, where the couple have often been portrayed as a symbol of stability amid the chaos of elite football.

His younger brother, Rodrigo — known as Digão — also became a professional footballer and spent time connected to Milan.

For Kaká, family has often been described as a grounding force, helping him navigate the pressures of fame, expectation and global celebrity.

---

### Injuries and the Fight Back

Though Kaká’s rise was dazzling, his career has not been without physical setbacks. His early spinal injury remains the most dramatic, but at Milan he has also had to manage recurring fitness issues, including knee and muscular problems that at times disrupted his rhythm.

Each return has reinforced the image of a player driven by more than ambition. Kaká’s game depends on acceleration and fluid movement; injuries threaten precisely those qualities. Yet he has repeatedly worked his way back, adapting when necessary and showing the resilience that has been part of his story since youth.

That resilience is one reason Milan supporters identify with him so strongly. Kaká is not just admired for what he does when fully fit; he is respected for the way he responds when challenged.

---

### A Cabinet Full of Honours

Kaká’s list of achievements already places him among the greats of his generation.

With Brazil, he won the 2002 FIFA World Cup and later the Confederations Cup. With AC Milan, he has won Serie A, the UEFA Champions League, the UEFA Super Cup and the FIFA Club World Cup.

Individually, his 2007 awards confirmed his status at the top of world football:
